context: Define the following:
solution: An **exocrine gland** is a gland that has a **duct**, through which its secretion is carried to a body surface or into a cavity, e.g., the salivary glands and the **exocrine pancreas**, which secretes pancreatic enzymes, water and bicarbonate ions.
groundedIn: §19.1; §19.2.8; §19.3 — endocrine glands lack ducts (contrast); pancreas is a composite gland, both exocrine and endocrine; secretin and CCK act on the exocrine pancreas; BEYOND CHAPTER: exocrine glands possess ducts carrying the secretion to a surface or cavity; salivary glands as an example

context: Define the following:
solution: An **endocrine gland** is a gland that lacks a duct (a **ductless gland**) and releases its secretion, called a **hormone**, directly into the blood, which transports it to a distantly located target organ, e.g., the thyroid and the pituitary.
groundedIn: §19.1; §19.2 — endocrine glands lack ducts and are hence called ductless glands; their secretions are hormones, released into the blood and transported to a distantly located target organ; pituitary, thyroid etc. are organised endocrine bodies

context: Define the following:
solution: **Hormones** are **non-nutrient chemicals** which act as **intercellular messengers** and are produced in **trace amounts**. (Classically, a hormone is a chemical produced by an endocrine gland and released into the blood, which transports it to a distantly located target organ.)
groundedIn: §19.1 — classical definition of hormone and the current scientific definition: non-nutrient chemicals which act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts

stem: Diagrammatically indicate the location of the various endocrine glands in our body.
solution:
**Diagram** (Fig. 19.1, book figure attached): an outline of the human body (head, neck and trunk) with each organised endocrine gland drawn in its position and labelled.

1. **Hypothalamus**: in the brain, the basal part of the diencephalon (forebrain).
2. **Pituitary**: just below the hypothalamus, in a bony cavity called the sella tursica, attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk.
3. **Pineal**: on the dorsal side of the forebrain.
4. **Thyroid**: in the neck, two lobes on either side of the trachea joined by the isthmus.
5. **Parathyroid**: four glands on the back side of the thyroid, one pair in each lobe (labelled together with the thyroid).
6. **Thymus**: in the chest, between the lungs behind the sternum, on the ventral side of the aorta.
7. **Pancreas**: in the abdomen, drawn as an elongated gland above the kidneys.
8. **Adrenal**: one gland at the anterior part (top) of each kidney.
9. **Ovary (in female)**: a pair in the lower abdomen.
10. **Testis (in male)**: a pair in the scrotal sac, outside the abdomen.

Labels a marker looks for: **hypothalamus, pituitary, pineal, thyroid and parathyroid, thymus, pancreas, adrenal, ovary (in female), testis (in male)**.
groundedIn: §19.2; Fig. 19.1; §19.2.1; §19.2.2; §19.2.3; §19.2.4; §19.2.5; §19.2.6; §19.2.7; §19.2.9; §19.2.10 — organised endocrine bodies and their figure; hypothalamus basal part of diencephalon; pituitary in sella tursica attached by a stalk; pineal dorsal side of forebrain; thyroid lobes either side of trachea; four parathyroids on the back of the thyroid; thymus between lungs behind sternum; adrenal at anterior part of each kidney; testis in scrotal sac; ovaries in abdomen

context: List the hormones secreted by the following:
solution:
The hypothalamus secretes two types of hormones that regulate the pituitary:

1. **Releasing hormones**, which stimulate secretion of pituitary hormones, e.g., **gonadotrophin releasing hormone (GnRH)**, thyrotrophin releasing hormone (TRH), corticotrophin releasing hormone (CRH) and growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH).
2. **Inhibiting hormones**, which inhibit secretion of pituitary hormones, e.g., **somatostatin**, which inhibits the release of growth hormone.

In addition, **oxytocin** and **vasopressin (ADH)** are synthesised by the hypothalamus and transported axonally to the neurohypophysis, which stores and releases them.
groundedIn: §19.2.1; §19.2.2 — releasing and inhibiting hormones; GnRH and somatostatin; oxytocin and vasopressin synthesised by the hypothalamus and transported axonally to the neurohypophysis; BEYOND CHAPTER: TRH, CRH and GHRH as further releasing hormones

context: List the hormones secreted by the following:
solution:
1. **Pars distalis (anterior pituitary):** **growth hormone (GH)**, **prolactin (PRL)**, **thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH)**, **adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH)**, **luteinizing hormone (LH)** and **follicle stimulating hormone (FSH)**.
2. **Pars intermedia:** only one hormone, **melanocyte stimulating hormone (MSH)**.
3. **Neurohypophysis (pars nervosa, posterior pituitary):** stores and releases **oxytocin** and **vasopressin (ADH)**, which are synthesised by the hypothalamus.
groundedIn: §19.2.2 — pars distalis produces GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH and FSH; pars intermedia secretes only MSH; neurohypophysis stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin synthesised by the hypothalamus

context: Write short notes on the functions of the following hormones:
solution:
**Parathyroid hormone (PTH)** is a peptide hormone secreted by the parathyroid glands; its secretion is regulated by the circulating level of calcium ions. It **increases the blood \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) level**:

1. It acts on **bones** and stimulates **bone resorption** (dissolution/demineralisation), releasing \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\).
2. It stimulates **reabsorption of \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\)** by the renal tubules.
3. It increases \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) **absorption from the digested food**.

PTH is therefore a **hypercalcemic hormone**. Along with **thyrocalcitonin (TCT)**, it plays a significant role in **calcium balance** in the body.
groundedIn: §19.2.5 — PTH secretion regulated by circulating Ca2+; PTH stimulates bone resorption, renal reabsorption of Ca2+ and Ca2+ absorption from digested food; hypercalcemic hormone; with TCT maintains calcium balance

context: Write short notes on the functions of the following hormones:
solution:
The thyroid hormones, **thyroxine (\(\text{T}_4\))** and **triiodothyronine (\(\text{T}_3\))**, have these functions:

1. They regulate the **basal metabolic rate (BMR)**.
2. They support **red blood cell formation** (erythropoiesis).
3. They control the **metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats**.
4. They influence the maintenance of **water and electrolyte balance**.
5. They are needed for the **development and maturation** of the central neural system; their deficiency during pregnancy causes **cretinism** in the baby.
6. They influence the **menstrual cycle**; hypothyroidism in adult women may make it irregular.

The thyroid also secretes **thyrocalcitonin (TCT)**, which regulates the blood calcium level by decreasing it.
groundedIn: §19.2.4 — thyroid hormones regulate BMR, support RBC formation, control metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats, influence water and electrolyte balance; hypothyroidism in pregnancy causes cretinism; irregular menstrual cycle in hypothyroidism; TCT regulates blood calcium; development and maturation of the central neural system and TCT lowering calcium (stated in the chapter Summary)

context: Write short notes on the functions of the following hormones:
solution:
**Thymosins** are peptide hormones secreted by the **thymus** gland.

1. They play a major role in the **differentiation of T-lymphocytes**, which provide **cell-mediated immunity**.
2. They also promote the **production of antibodies**, which provide **humoral immunity**.
3. The thymus degenerates in old individuals, so thymosin production decreases and the **immune responses of old persons become weak**.
groundedIn: §19.2.6 — thymosins play a major role in the differentiation of T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity), promote antibody production (humoral immunity); thymus degenerates in old individuals and immune responses weaken

context: Write short notes on the functions of the following hormones:
solution:
**Androgens**, mainly **testosterone**, are secreted by the **Leydig cells** (interstitial cells) of the testis.

1. They regulate the **development, maturation and functions of the male accessory sex organs**, such as epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate gland and urethra.
2. They stimulate **muscular growth**, growth of facial and axillary hair, aggressiveness and low pitch of voice (**male secondary sex characters**).
3. They play a major stimulatory role in **spermatogenesis**.
4. They act on the central neural system and influence **male sexual behaviour (libido)**.
5. They produce **anabolic** (synthetic) effects on protein and carbohydrate metabolism.
groundedIn: §19.2.9 — androgens from Leydig cells regulate the male accessory sex organs, stimulate muscular growth, facial and axillary hair, aggressiveness, low pitch of voice, spermatogenesis, libido, and anabolic effects

context: Write short notes on the functions of the following hormones:
solution:
**Estrogens** are steroid hormones synthesised and secreted mainly by the **growing ovarian follicles**. Their actions:

1. Stimulation of growth and activities of the **female secondary sex organs**.
2. Development of the **growing ovarian follicles**.
3. Appearance of **female secondary sex characters**, e.g., high pitch of voice.
4. **Mammary gland development**.
5. Regulation of **female sexual behaviour**.
groundedIn: §19.2.10 — estrogen secreted mainly by growing ovarian follicles; stimulates growth and activities of female secondary sex organs, development of growing follicles, female secondary sex characters, mammary gland development, regulates female sexual behaviour

context: Write short notes on the functions of the following hormones:
solution:
Insulin and glucagon are peptide hormones of the **Islets of Langerhans** of the pancreas; together they maintain **glucose homeostasis** in blood.

**Insulin** (from \(\beta\)-cells):

1. Acts mainly on **hepatocytes** and **adipocytes** and enhances cellular **glucose uptake and utilisation**.
2. Glucose moves rapidly from blood into these cells, so the blood glucose level falls (**hypoglycemia**).
3. Stimulates conversion of glucose to glycogen (**glycogenesis**) in the target cells.

**Glucagon** (from \(\alpha\)-cells):

1. Acts mainly on liver cells (hepatocytes) and stimulates **glycogenolysis**, increasing blood sugar (**hyperglycemia**).
2. Stimulates **gluconeogenesis**, which also raises blood sugar.
3. Reduces cellular glucose uptake and utilisation.

Thus insulin is a **hypoglycemic** and glucagon a **hyperglycemic** hormone. Prolonged hyperglycemia leads to **diabetes mellitus**.
groundedIn: §19.2.8 — glucagon from alpha-cells acts on hepatocytes, stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, reduces glucose uptake, hyperglycemic; insulin from beta-cells acts on hepatocytes and adipocytes, enhances glucose uptake and utilisation, glycogenesis, hypoglycemia; glucose homeostasis maintained jointly; prolonged hyperglycemia leads to diabetes mellitus

context: Which hormonal deficiency is responsible for the following:
solution: Deficiency of **insulin** (and/or insulin resistance). The resulting prolonged hyperglycemia causes diabetes mellitus, with loss of glucose through urine and formation of ketone bodies.

context: Which hormonal deficiency is responsible for the following:
solution: Deficiency of the **thyroid hormones** (thyroxine, \(\text{T}_4\), and \(\text{T}_3\)), i.e., **hypothyroidism**, caused by deficiency of **iodine** in the diet; the thyroid gland enlarges.
groundedIn: §19.2.4 — iodine is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis; iodine deficiency results in hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid gland, goitre

context: Which hormonal deficiency is responsible for the following:
solution: Deficiency of the **thyroid hormones** (**hypothyroidism**) **during pregnancy**, which causes defective development and maturation of the growing baby: stunted growth, mental retardation, low intelligence quotient, abnormal skin and deaf-mutism.
groundedIn: §19.2.4 — hypothyroidism during pregnancy causes defective development of the growing baby leading to stunted growth (cretinism), mental retardation, low IQ, abnormal skin, deaf-mutism

stem: Briefly mention the mechanism of action of FSH.
solution:
**FSH** is a pituitary hormone and so a **protein (peptide) hormone**; it acts through **membrane-bound receptors** and **second messengers**.

1. FSH, released by the anterior pituitary, reaches its target cells in the **gonads** through blood.
2. It binds to its specific **receptor on the cell membrane** of the target cell, forming a **hormone-receptor complex**. The hormone does not enter the cell.
3. The complex generates **second messengers** (e.g., **cyclic AMP**) inside the cell.
4. The second messengers regulate **cellular metabolism**, producing the physiological response:
   - in females, **growth and development of the ovarian follicles**;
   - in males, regulation of **spermatogenesis** (together with androgens).
groundedIn: §19.2.2; §19.4; Fig. 19.5 — FSH from the pars distalis stimulates growth of ovarian follicles and, with androgens, regulates spermatogenesis; pituitary hormones are peptide/protein hormones; membrane-bound receptors, hormone-receptor complex, second messengers such as cyclic AMP regulating cellular metabolism

stem:
Match the following:

| Column I | Column II |
|---|---|
| (a) \(\text{T}_4\) | (i) Hypothalamus |
| (b) PTH | (ii) Thyroid |
| (c) GnRH | (iii) Pituitary |
| (d) LH | (iv) Parathyroid |
solution:
(a) - (ii), (b) - (iv), (c) - (i), (d) - (iii)

| Column I | Column II |
|---|---|
| (a) \(\text{T}_4\) | (ii) Thyroid |
| (b) PTH | (iv) Parathyroid |
| (c) GnRH | (i) Hypothalamus |
| (d) LH | (iii) Pituitary |

- **\(\text{T}_4\)** (thyroxine) is synthesised by the follicular cells of the **thyroid**.
- **PTH** (parathyroid hormone) is secreted by the **parathyroid** glands.
- **GnRH** (gonadotrophin releasing hormone) is a releasing hormone of the **hypothalamus**.
- **LH** (luteinizing hormone) is produced by the pars distalis of the **pituitary**.
groundedIn: §19.2.4; §19.2.5; §19.2.1; §19.2.2 — thyroid follicular cells synthesise T4; parathyroid glands secrete PTH; GnRH is a hypothalamic hormone; pars distalis produces LH
